<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:main}
There is a minimal two-tetrahedron triangulation $\mathcal T$ of $L(3,1)$
such that
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $\mathcal T$ has a null-homotopic loop edge;
\item[(ii)] $\mathcal T$ supports no cluster of three 2-quad-type solutions;
\item[(iii)] $\mathcal T$ supports no solution to Thurston's equation;
\item[(iv)] every maximum of $\operatorname{vol}\colon\operatorname{SAS}(\mathcal T)\to\mathbb R$ is smooth.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently, $\mathcal T$ is a counterexample to (C1), (C2), and (C3).
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rmk:scope}
These conclusions concern the conjectures as stated.
Since $L(3,1)$ is not simply
connected, the example does not address the restricted versions used
in Luo's proposed approach to the Poincar\'e conjecture.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:support}
Let $v\ne0$ satisfy $Wv=0$ and have at most two nonzero
coordinates. Then $\operatorname{supp}(v)=\{x_1,y_1\}$. In fact, $v$ is a
nonzero multiple of $(1,0,0,1,0,0)^{\mathsf T}$.
In particular, $\mathcal T$ supports no cluster of three 2-quad-type solutions.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
A kernel vector supported on one coordinate would give a zero
column of $W$, and one supported on two coordinates would give a
proportional pair of columns. In \eqref{eq:matching} no column is
zero, and the only proportional pair consists of the $x_1$- and
$y_1$-columns, which are negatives of one another. This proves
the assertion about $v$.

Let $z$ be a 2-quad-type solution and let $v$ be its quadrilateral
projection. Then $v\ne0$, $Wv=0$, and $v$ has at most two nonzero
coordinates, so the preceding calculation gives
$\operatorname{supp}(v)=\{x_1,y_1\}$. Thus
every 2-quad-type solution vanishes at $x_2,x_3,y_2,y_3$, so
neither tetrahedron supplies the three distinguished quadrilateral
types required by a cluster. Hence no such cluster exists.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:thurston}
The triangulation $\mathcal T$ supports no solution to Thurston's equation.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Suppose that such a shape assignment $\zeta$ exists, and put
$z=\zeta(x_1)$ and $w=\zeta(y_1)$. Here $x_i$ and $y_i$ are the
quadrilateral types in $A$ and $B$ defined in
Section~\ref{sec:quadrilaterals}. In particular,
$z,w\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0,1\}$, and
\[
\begin{aligned}
\bigl(\zeta(x_1),\zeta(x_2),\zeta(x_3)\bigr)
&=\left(z,\frac{1}{1-z},\frac{z-1}{z}\right),\\
\bigl(\zeta(y_1),\zeta(y_2),\zeta(y_3)\bigr)
&=\left(w,\frac{1}{1-w},\frac{w-1}{w}\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
The edge equations at $a,b,c$, read from the incidence matrix in
Section~\ref{sec:quadrilaterals}, are
\begin{align*}
zw&=1,\\
\left(\frac{1}{1-z}\right)^2w
\left(\frac{w-1}{w}\right)^2&=1,\\
z\left(\frac{z-1}{z}\right)^2
\left(\frac{1}{1-w}\right)^2&=1.
\end{align*}
The first gives $w=z^{-1}$. Substituting into the last two reduces
their left-hand sides to $z^{-1}$ and $z$, respectively. They force
$z=1$, which is forbidden. Hence no solution exists.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{rmk:generalized-thurston}
Luo's generalized Thurston equation \cite[Section 3.2]{Luo2011}
allows edge products $\pm1$. Taking $z=w=-1$ gives the shape triple
$(-1,\tfrac12,2)$ in each tetrahedron, with edge products $(1,-1,-1)$
at $(a,b,c)$. Thus the generalized equation has a solution, and the
example does not contradict \cite[Theorem 1.2]{Luo2011}.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{rmk:thurston-theorem}
Proposition~\ref{prop:thurston} also follows from the
Segerman--Tillmann theorem \cite[Theorem 1.1]{Luo2011}, since
$a$ is a null-homotopic loop edge by
Section~\ref{sec:triangulation}.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:volume}
Every maximum of $\operatorname{vol}\colon\operatorname{SAS}(\mathcal T)\to\mathbb R$ is smooth.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Suppose that a non-smooth maximum exists. By the Futer--Gu\'eritaud
theorem, as stated in \cite[Theorem 4.4]{Luo2011}, we may choose a
non-smooth maximum $\widetilde u$ such that, in each tetrahedron,
if one quadrilateral parameter belongs to $\{1,-1\}$, then all
three do. Since $\widetilde u$ is non-smooth, there is a tetrahedron
$\sigma$ whose three quadrilateral types $q_1,q_2,q_3$ satisfy
$\widetilde u(q_i)\in\{1,-1\}$ for $i=1,2,3$.
By \cite[Theorem 4.2(a)]{Luo2011}, each quadrilateral taking the value
$\pm1$ at such a maximum has a nonzero coordinate in some
2-quad-type solution of Haken's equations. Applying this result to
$q_1,q_2,q_3$ gives solutions $z_1,z_2,z_3$ with $z_i(q_i)\ne0$.
These form a cluster, contradicting
Lemma~\ref{lem:support}. Hence every maximum is smooth.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Section~\ref{sec:triangulation} constructs $\mathcal T$ as a minimal
triangulation of $L(3,1)$ and proves (i);
Lemma~\ref{lem:support} proves (ii); and
Propositions~\ref{prop:thurston} and~\ref{prop:volume} prove
(iii) and (iv). The manifold $L(3,1)$ is closed, orientable, and
irreducible, so all the required hypotheses hold. Now (ii)--(iii)
refute (C1), (iii)--(iv) refute (C2), and (i)--(ii) refute (C3).
<!-- end proof-4 -->
